summary: Describes a mechanism for QUIC clients and servers to select a mutually supported version. When the first flight formats are compatible, negotiation can happen without an extra round trip. It updates the QUIC documents it builds on.

eli5.summary: Two people figure out a language both understand. If they are lucky, they work it out in the first sentence without extra back-and-forth.

questions: how does quic pick a version
quic version negotiation without extra round trip
what is quic compatible version negotiation
how does quic prevent version downgrade
subtitle: How QUIC endpoints agree on a version, with no extra round trip when versions are compatible.

tldr.problem: QUIC version 1 lets a server say the client's version is unacceptable, but gives the client no safe way to use that information to pick a version both sides support.
tldr.mechanism: Endpoints exchange a Version Information structure in the handshake. Compatible versions can be negotiated within one connection, and incompatible ones use a Version Negotiation packet and a second connection, with checks against downgrade attacks.
tldr.outcome: Clients and servers can select a mutually supported version, and the round trip is saved when the first flights are compatible. The RFC updates RFC 8999.

today: RFC 9368 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 8999.

sections.title: Why QUIC Needs Version Negotiation
sections.content:
The QUIC invariants (RFC 8999) define a Version Negotiation packet but not how an endpoint reacts to one. QUIC version 1 (RFC 9000) lets a server use it to say the client's version is unacceptable, but does not let the client safely act on that to start a new connection.

This RFC defines two mechanisms. Incompatible negotiation uses Version Negotiation packets, works for all versions and costs an extra round trip. Compatible negotiation saves the round trip but only applies when versions are compatible. The RFC updates RFC 8999.
sections.eli5: If you speak a language the other person does not know, you have to try again with another one. This RFC says how to pick a shared one safely.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
The first flight is the set of packets the client sends before hearing from the server. The Chosen Version is the version of that first flight. The Original Version is the version of the very first packet the client sends, and the Negotiated Version is the one in use once negotiation completes.

Version A is compatible with B if a first flight from A can be converted into a first flight from B. Compatibility is not symmetric. A new version is assumed compatible with nothing unless a document says otherwise, and implementations MUST NOT assume compatibility.
sections.eli5: Two languages are compatible if you can translate the opening sentence from one to the other without losing the meaning.

sections.title: How the Two Kinds of Negotiation Work
sections.content:
In incompatible negotiation, a server that cannot parse the client's first flight sends a Version Negotiation packet listing its Offered Versions. The client picks a version it supports and sends a new first flight, or aborts if there is none. Only servers can start it: clients MUST NOT send Version Negotiation packets and servers MUST ignore any they receive.

In compatible negotiation, the server parses the first flight, reads the client's list of compatible versions, and MUST select one it supports and knows the client's Chosen Version is compatible with. It converts the first flight to that version and replies as if it had received it, all within the same connection. If conversion fails, it MUST abort the handshake. A client can disable this by listing only its Chosen Version.

The client SHOULD choose its Original Version to avoid incompatible negotiation, for example the oldest version it supports while advertising newer compatible versions.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the server says: that language is unknown, try one of these. Other times it just answers in a better language you both know.

sections.title: Version Information
sections.content:
Endpoints exchange Version Information during the handshake, made of a Chosen Version and a list of Available Versions, each 32 bits. In QUIC version 1 it travels in the version_information transport parameter, which is authenticated.

When sent by a client, Available Versions lists all versions the first flight is compatible with, in descending preference, and must include the Chosen Version. The preference is only advisory. When sent by a server, it lists the Fully Deployed Versions, in no meaningful order, and it MAY be empty. Both sides MAY include reserved versions of the form 0x?a?a?a?a to exercise negotiation.
sections.eli5: Each side hands over a note: the language I picked, and the other languages I can also speak.

sections.title: Server Fleets and Rolling Updates
sections.content:
Large deployments run many server instances that are not updated at the same moment. The RFC defines three sets: Acceptable Versions (what an instance will use), Offered Versions (what it lists in a Version Negotiation packet) and Fully Deployed Versions (supported by every instance).

To avoid false downgrade alarms from stale packets, operators SHOULD add a version in three steps: Acceptable first, then Offered, then Fully Deployed, waiting at least one Maximum Segment Lifetime (RECOMMENDED value: one minute) between steps. Removal goes in the reverse order. During the update window, connections are vulnerable to downgrade for versions that are not Fully Deployed.
sections.eli5: When a school adds a new language class, it first trains every teacher, then announces it, then makes it official, waiting between steps.

sections.title: Application Protocols and Future Versions
sections.content:
A client only considers versions that support its intended application protocols. If the first flight advertises several ALPN tokens, the server MUST pick only a token that can run over the version it selects. An existing ALPN token MUST NOT be used with a different QUIC version unless that version supports the needed transport features and ALPN, and the original version is compatible with it.

Designers of future versions SHOULD try to make commonly deployed versions compatible with theirs. Any document that makes versions compatible must say how Retry and 0-RTT packets are handled, and new versions using TLS 1.3 SHOULD scope session tickets to one QUIC version.
sections.eli5: Not every game can be played in every language, so the server only picks a pairing that works.

sections.title: Downgrade Prevention and Security
sections.content:
A version downgrade is an attack that makes endpoints use a different version than they would have without the attacker. Clients MUST ignore Version Negotiation packets that contain the Original Version. Both endpoints MUST parse the peer's Version Information and close the connection on a parsing failure, and a Chosen Version or Available Version of zero is a failure.

If the client acted on a Version Negotiation packet, it MUST check that it would have picked the same version had it seen the server's Available Versions. If not, or if that field is empty, it MUST close the connection with a version negotiation error. Clients also MUST check that the server's Chosen Version equals the Negotiated Version.

The mechanism relies on Version Information being authenticated, which transport parameters are in QUIC version 1. Compatible versions get the security of the weakest common version, and the RFC says more analysis of cross-protocol attacks is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The two sides compare notes inside a sealed envelope, so a trickster cannot fool them into using an older, weaker language.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the version_information transport parameter with value 0x11. It also registered the transport error code VERSION_NEGOTIATION_ERROR with value 0x11, described as an error negotiating the version. Both have status permanent.
sections.eli5: The official lists now have the new setting and the new error name, each with its own number.
